questions.q: A 45-year-old farmer presents with a painful, rapidly enlarging ulcer on his right forearm after handling cattle. The lesion has a black eschar at the center with non-pitting edema and is painless despite appearing severe. The surrounding skin shows a "gelatinous" quality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (malignant pustule) classically presents with a painless black eschar with extensive gelatinous non-pitting edema, occurring after contact with Bacillus anthracis from animal products. The painlessness despite severe appearance is characteristic.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of bright red follicular papules and pustules on her trunk after hot tub use. The lesions spare the face and worsen after bathing. Culture grows gram-negative rods. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Hot tub folliculitis is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa (serotype O:11), which thrives in warm water environments. It presents 8-48 hours after exposure with pruritic follicular papules/pustules predominantly on areas covered by swimwear. It is usually self-limiting.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man from rural Maharashtra presents with painless nodular thickening along the ulnar nerve and loss of sensation over the little and ring fingers. Skin scraping from an ear lobe shows 5+ bacterial index. Histopathology shows solid-staining bacilli in globi within foamy macrophages. What is the leprosy type?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) presents with high bacillary load (bacterial index 4-6+), globi of bacilli within foamy (Virchow) macrophages, widespread symmetric skin involvement, and nerve thickening. The immune response is dominated by Th2 cells with high antibody but poor cell-mediated immunity.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man on multi-drug therapy for leprosy develops sudden high fever, painful tender erythematous nodules on his trunk and limbs, uveitis, and orchitis. His skin biopsy shows neutrophilic infiltration in the dermis with intact bacilli. What reaction is this?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction with systemic features including fever, uveitis, orchitis, and tender erythematous nodules. Histology shows neutrophilic infiltrate with intact bacilli.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with deeply hyperpigmented, velvety skin in her axillae, neck, and groin. She has a BMI of 38 and irregular menstrual cycles. Her fasting glucose is 110 mg/dL. Which skin marker is she displaying?
questions.exp: Acanthosis nigricans presents as velvety hyperpigmented plaques in body folds and is strongly associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and PCOS. Elevated insulin stimulates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes causing epidermal hyperplasia. Histology shows papillomatosis and mild hyperkeratosis.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with Gottron's papules over the MCP and PIP joints, heliotrope rash with periorbital edema, and proximal muscle weakness. Her CK is markedly elevated. Skin biopsy shows vacuolar interface changes with mucin deposition. The most characteristic nail fold finding is:
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis classically shows dilated, tortuous nail fold capillary loops with avascular areas (dropout) on capillaroscopy. This, along with Gottron's papules, heliotrope rash, elevated muscle enzymes, and interface dermatitis, constitutes the diagnostic criteria. NF-NXP2 and anti-MDA5 are associated antibodies.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with a history of three spontaneous abortions presents with a malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and a prolonged APTT. ANA is positive (1:640, speckled pattern). Which antibody is most specific for SLE?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm antibodies are the most specific antibody for SLE (specificity ~99%), though not highly sensitive (~25%). Anti-dsDNA is also specific and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and SCLE. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with tense blisters on normal and erythematous skin of the trunk and thighs with intense pruritus. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear IgG and C3 along the dermoepidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid presents in older patients with tense blisters (subepidermal), negative Nikolsky sign, and intense pruritus. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. The target antigens are BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 on hemidesmosomes. It is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters that rupture easily leaving painful erosions predominantly involving the oral mucosa and upper trunk. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows intercellular IgG deposits in the epidermis (fish-net/chicken-wire pattern). Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris primarily targets Desmoglein 3 (mucosal type) and both Dsg3 and Dsg1 (mucocutaneous type). It presents with flaccid blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, and intercellular IgG on DIF. Oral involvement is the hallmark initial presentation. It is an acantholytic disorder.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman from Rajasthan presents with grouped pruritic vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. She has a history of malabsorption and folate deficiency. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal blisters with neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillae tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy (celiac disease), causing malabsorption. It presents with grouped, intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces. DIF shows granular IgA at dermal papillae tips (pathognomonic). Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies are positive. Dapsone is the treatment of choice.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man presents with widespread reddish-brown maculopapular rash involving the palms and soles, painless oral mucous patches, and diffuse lymphadenopathy. His RPR is 1:256. What stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Secondary syphilis occurs 4-8 weeks after the primary chancre and is characterized by disseminated maculopapular rash (including palms and soles), condylomata lata, mucous patches, alopecia (moth-eaten pattern), and lymphadenopathy. High RPR titers confirm active infection. It is the most infectious stage.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with painless, irregular, wart-like lesions in the perianal area that have a moist, cauliflower appearance. They are highly infectious. Biopsy shows koilocytic changes. Which HPV types are most commonly responsible for condylomata acuminata?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (anogenital warts) are caused predominantly by low-risk HPV types 6 and 11. High-risk types 16 and 18 cause cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal cancers. HPV 1 and 2 cause common warts (verruca vulgaris). HPV 31 and 33 are also high-risk types associated with cervical dysplasia.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse presents with a painless, well-defined, indurated ulcer with clean base on the glans penis. VDRL is non-reactive but TPHA is reactive. Dark field microscopy is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Primary syphilitic chancre is a painless, indurated ulcer with a clean, non-purulent base caused by Treponema pallidum. VDRL may be non-reactive in early primary syphilis (serological window period). TPHA (treponemal test) becomes positive earlier and remains positive for life. Dark field microscopy showing spirochetes is diagnostic.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with a well-demarcated, silvery-scaled plaque on her elbow with positive Auspitz sign and positive Koebner phenomenon. On removing the scale, pinpoint bleeding is seen. Histopathology shows parakeratosis, Munro's microabscesses, and elongated rete ridges. What is the pathological hallmark of psoriasis?
questions.exp: Both Munro's microabscesses (collections of neutrophils in the parakeratotic stratum corneum) and Spongiform pustule of Kogoj (neutrophilic collections within the spinous layer, seen in pustular psoriasis) are characteristic histological findings. Pautrier's microabscesses are seen in mycosis fungoides. Munro's is the most classic chronic plaque finding.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man on methotrexate for psoriasis develops progressive dyspnea and a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows bilateral reticular opacities. Which complication of methotrexate is this?
questions.exp: Methotrexate pneumonitis is an idiosyncratic, potentially fatal complication that can occur at any dose and time point. It presents with dyspnea, dry cough, and fever. Chest imaging shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. It requires immediate discontinuation of methotrexate. Liver toxicity (hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis) is the most common serious complication requiring liver biopsy monitoring.

questions.q: A 20-year-old woman on dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis develops pallor, jaundice, and shortness of breath. CBC shows hemoglobin of 7 g/dL with Heinz bodies on peripheral smear. What is the mechanism of dapsone-induced hemolysis?
opts: Oxidative hemolysis due to G6PD deficiency or dapsone metabolites
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent oxidative hemolysis through its hydroxylamine metabolite (dapsone hydroxylamine), which oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin and causes Heinz body formation (denatured hemoglobin). G6PD deficiency exacerbates this. Methemoglobinemia and hemolytic anemia are the two major hematological side effects of dapsone.

questions.q: A 19-year-old boy on isotretinoin for nodulocystic acne asks about contraception counseling for his girlfriend. Which teratogenic effect is most feared with isotretinoin?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Pregnancy Category X). It causes retinoic acid embryopathy including craniofacial defects (microtia, microcephaly), cardiovascular malformations (conotruncal defects), CNS abnormalities (hydrocephalus, microcephaly), and thymic aplasia. It requires two negative pregnancy tests before starting and two forms of contraception.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer presents with a painless, pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on the nasolabial fold with a central depression (rolled border). He has decades of sun exposure. Biopsy shows palisading tumor cells at the periphery with retraction artifact. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy. The nodular type presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias, rolled borders, and central ulceration. Histology shows palisading basaloid cells at tumor periphery with retraction artifact. It arises from the basal layer and rarely metastasizes, but is locally invasive.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with an irregularly pigmented lesion on his back with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation (black, brown, red), and diameter of 9 mm. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. Biopsy confirms malignant melanoma. What is the most important prognostic factor?
questions.exp: Breslow thickness (vertical depth of invasion in millimeters from the granular layer) is the single most important prognostic factor in melanoma and determines staging, sentinel lymph node biopsy eligibility, and survival. Clark level (anatomic level of invasion) is used in thin melanomas (<1mm). Ulceration is also an important prognostic factor affecting T staging.

questions.q: A 70-year-old woman with extensive sun damage presents with an erythematous, scaly plaque on her cheek that has been growing for 2 years. Biopsy shows full-thickness dysplasia of the epidermis without dermal invasion. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bowen's disease (SCC in situ) presents as a slowly enlarging, well-demarcated, erythematous scaly plaque. Histology shows full-thickness epidermal dysplasia (atypical keratinocytes involving the full epidermis) without dermal invasion. It has ~3-5% risk of progression to invasive SCC. Actinic keratosis shows partial-thickness dysplasia.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman from Assam presents with a painless, progressive swelling of her lower leg with woody fibrosis and multiple papillomatous nodules. The overlying skin has a 'peau d'orange' appearance. Lymphoscintigraphy confirms lymphatic obstruction. Microscopy of skin biopsy shows thick-walled vessels with endothelial hyperplasia. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Brugia malayi causes lymphatic filariasis in Southeast Asia and South India, leading to lymphedema and elephantiasis. It primarily affects the lower limbs, unlike W. bancrofti which also affects genitalia. Microfilariae are sub-periodic in B. malayi vs nocturnal periodic in W. bancrofti. Skin changes in elephantiasis include 'peau d'orange' appearance and papillomatosis.

questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, progressive ulcer on his right shin that started as a papule after minor trauma. The ulcer has undermined edges, a boggy necrotic base, and surrounding granulomatous induration. AFB stain of the wound discharge is positive. Which organism is responsible?
questions.exp: Buruli ulcer is caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, which produces mycolactone toxin causing tissue necrosis. It presents as a painless ulcer with undermined edges, most commonly on the lower limbs. AFB stain of exudate is positive. PCR is the gold standard for diagnosis. WHO-recommended treatment is rifampicin plus clarithromycin or amikacin.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with a verrucous, warty plaque on his forearm. Biopsy shows black, pigmented fungal cells (medlar/sclerotic bodies/Fumagoid cells) with a 'copper penny' appearance. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by pigmented (dematiaceous) fungi (Fonsecaea, Cladophialophora, Phialophora) and presents with verrucous, cauliflower-like plaques. Pathognomonic finding is Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells/copper pennies) — thick-walled, dark brown cells that divide by cross-wall formation, seen on KOH prep and biopsy. Itraconazole is the treatment of choice.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with painless, non-pruritic hypopigmented macules on his trunk. KOH preparation shows 'spaghetti and meatball' appearance (short hyphal segments and round spores). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now called Malassezia globosa/restricta), a lipophilic dimorphic yeast. KOH preparation shows the classic 'spaghetti and meatball' (short hyphae + spores). Wood's lamp shows golden-yellow fluorescence. The yeast phase causes hypopigmentation by producing azelaic acid, which inhibits melanin synthesis.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic man presents with a rapidly spreading, painful erythema and edema of the scrotum and perineum with crepitations on palpation. CT scan shows gas in the fascial planes. The most critical initial management is:
opts: Urgent surgical debridement plus IV antibiotics
questions.exp: Fournier's gangrene is a life-threatening necrotizing fasciitis of the genitoperineal region caused by synergistic polymicrobial infection. The hallmark is gas in fascial planes on imaging (CT). Treatment requires emergency aggressive surgical debridement (debridement is the cornerstone), combined with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobes). Delay in surgery is the main predictor of mortality.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a suspicious pigmented lesion. Dermoscopy reveals an atypical vascular pattern and the dermatologist performs a shave biopsy. The histopathology report requires staging. To determine the T stage in melanoma staging (AJCC 8th edition), which two parameters are essential?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition melanoma T staging is based on Breslow thickness (determining T1-T4) and ulceration (determining 'a' vs 'b' sub-classification). Mitotic rate is no longer used for T staging (it was removed from the 8th edition). Clark level is used only for T1a designation in thin melanomas without ulceration in the 7th edition but is not used in the 8th edition.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents for patch testing to evaluate occupational contact dermatitis. After applying the patch test, the reading at 48 hours shows erythema only, which clears by 96 hours. How should this reaction be interpreted?
questions.exp: In patch testing, a reaction showing only faint erythema (macular) that fades by 96 hours is classified as a doubtful/irritant reaction (?+). A true allergic reaction (1+) shows erythema + induration + papules; 2+ shows erythema + induration + papules + vesicles; 3+ shows bullous/spreading reaction. Reactions that grow stronger at 96 hours suggest Type IV hypersensitivity.

questions.q: A 10-year-old boy presents with annular erythematous patches with scaling at the periphery and central clearing on his trunk. Wood's lamp examination is negative. KOH preparation of scales from the advancing border shows fragmented hyphae. Which topical antifungal would be most appropriate first-line therapy?
questions.exp: Tinea corporis (ringworm) is treated with topical azole antifungals (clotrimazole, miconazole, ketoconazole) or allylamines (terbinafine) as first-line for localized disease. Nystatin is effective only against Candida species, not dermatophytes. Griseofulvin is not available in topical formulation for systemic use. Terbinafine topical is actually the most effective topical agent.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with crops of vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution on his left thorax, associated with severe burning pain. He had chickenpox at age 8. What is the pathophysiology of herpes zoster?
opts: Primary infection with VZV through respiratory droplets in adulthood
Reactivation of latent VZV from dorsal root ganglia
Superinfection with a different strain of VZV
questions.exp: Herpes zoster (shingles) results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV) that remains latent in dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia after primary varicella infection. Reactivation occurs due to waning cell-mediated immunity (aging, immunosuppression). It presents as dermatomal vesicular eruption with prodromal burning pain. Post-herpetic neuralgia is the most common complication.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with multiple skin-colored, dome-shaped, umbilicated papules on the trunk and axillae. They are 2-5 mm in diameter and express a white, cheesy material when squeezed. Giemsa-stained smear of the expressed material shows large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson bodies). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum is caused by Molluscipoxvirus (a poxvirus). It presents with characteristic umbilicated, pearlescent papules. Histology shows large intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies (Henderson-Paterson/molluscum bodies) representing viral factories that displace the nucleus. It is transmitted by direct contact and is self-limiting in immunocompetent children within 6-12 months.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with a firm, non-tender, rubbery lymph node in the right inguinal region. Six weeks earlier, he had a painless genital ulcer that has healed. He now has bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy with a groove sign (groove of Poupart's ligament dividing the nodes). Frei test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The secondary stage features inguinal buboes with pathognomonic 'groove sign' (lymph nodes above and below the inguinal ligament creating a groove). The Frei test (intradermal injection of LGV antigen — now obsolete) was historically positive. Current diagnosis by PCR or complement fixation test.
